It reads: “H is minus the sum, over the classes, of p sub c times the base-two logarithm of p sub c”, where $p_c$ is the proportion of class $c$ at that node.

With two classes it is between 0 and 1 bit. It is 0 when everything is of the same class — there is nothing to ask — and 1 when it is half and half, which is the maximum possible doubt. It is exactly the same formula with which the size of a message was measured, now applied to “how much doubt is left”.
Se lee: <em>«la ganancia es la entropía:
It reads: “the gain is the parent's entropy minus the sum, over the children, of n sub i over n, times the entropy of child i”.

The weight $n_i/n$ matters: splitting a group of a hundred into one of ninety-nine and one of one informs almost nothing, even if that one ends up perfectly pure. The gain is never negative and never exceeds the parent's entropy; if it equals it, the question has separated the classes perfectly and the tree ends there.
Se lee: <em>«la varianza de la media de:
It reads: “the variance of the mean of k functions is rho times sigma squared, plus one minus rho over k, times sigma squared”.

$\sigma^2$ is the variance of a single tree and $\rho$ is how alike they are to each other. If they were independent ($\rho = 0$) the variance would be divided by $k$ and putting in many would be enough. But they are alike, and there lies the method's trick: the two doses of randomness — the sample and the columns — exist to lower $\rho$, not to improve each tree. The first term is the floor: however many trees are put in, you do not get below $\rho\sigma^2$.
